misconceptions.description: Treating NIST AI RMF as optional paperwork because it is not legally binding
misconceptions.trigger: learner skips RMF practices because they are voluntary
misconceptions.feedback: RMF voluntariness changes its enforcement, not its operational value. RMF artifacts substantially overlap EU AI Act high-risk obligations and produce auditable evidence required by procurement and enterprise customers.

misconceptions.description: Assuming the EU AI Act only applies to companies headquartered in the EU
misconceptions.trigger: learner claims a US-based deployment is exempt
misconceptions.feedback: Brussels effect: any AI system whose output is used in the EU falls in scope. Headquarters location does not determine applicability. GDPR set this precedent; the AI Act follows it.

misconceptions.description: Believing the three governance frameworks are redundant and one suffices
misconceptions.trigger: learner cites only one framework and dismisses the others
misconceptions.feedback: They differ in scope (system vs organization vs society), enforceability (binding vs voluntary vs normative), and emphasis (UNESCO adds sustainability/equity/literacy). Treat one as primary and the others as cross-checks.

misconceptions.description: Believing ISO 42001 certification replaces compliance with binding regulation
misconceptions.trigger: learner cites ISO 42001 as the only compliance evidence
misconceptions.feedback: ISO 42001 is an auditable management system that helps demonstrate alignment but does not replace EU AI Act obligations or NIST RMF practices. It is the bridge, not the destination.
